name: Bubble sort
about: Sweeps the array swapping neighbours, so the largest unsorted item bubbles to the end of each pass.

name: Cocktail shaker sort
about: Bubble sort that sweeps in both directions, which moves small items near the end to the front much faster.

name: Odd-even sort
about: Compares all odd-even pairs, then all even-odd pairs. Each pair is independent, so it was designed for parallel processors.

name: Gnome sort
about: A garden gnome sorts flower pots: step forward while they're in order, swap and step back when they aren't. One loop, no nesting.

name: Comb sort
about: Bubble sort with a gap that shrinks by 1.3 each pass, which clears out small items stuck near the end. Very fast in practice for its simplicity.

name: Exchange sort
about: Compares every pair and swaps the ones out of order. The sort most people invent first.

name: Selection sort
about: Finds the smallest remaining item and puts it next. Always does the same comparisons, but at most n swaps.

name: Double selection sort
about: Selection sort that finds the smallest and largest in one pass and places both, so each pass closes in from each end.

name: Bingo sort
about: Selection sort that moves every copy of the current smallest value in one pass. With k distinct values it needs k passes, so duplicates make it fast.

name: Cycle sort
about: Counts how many items are smaller to find each item's exact final spot. It writes the fewest times possible, which matters on flash memory.

name: Pancake sort
about: The only move allowed is flipping a prefix, like a spatula under a stack of pancakes. Bill Gates co-wrote a research paper on this problem in 1979.

name: Insertion sort
about: Takes each item and slides it left into place, like sorting cards in your hand. Faster than anything else on tiny arrays, so fast sorts use it to finish.

name: Binary insertion sort
about: Insertion sort that binary-searches for the spot. It cuts comparisons to n log n, but items still have to shift.

name: Shell sort
about: Insertion sort on items a gap apart, halving the gap each round as Donald Shell did in 1959. Far items take big jumps early.

name: Shell sort (Ciura gaps)
about: The same algorithm with gaps found by experiment: 1, 4, 10, 23, 57, 132, 301, 701. Nobody has proved its average case, which is rare for such short code.

name: Library sort
about: Insertion sort that leaves gaps on the shelf, the way a librarian does, so inserting rarely has to shift much.

name: Merge sort (top-down)
about: Sorts each half recursively, then merges them. Von Neumann described it in 1945, and it never has a bad case.

name: Merge sort (bottom-up)
about: The same merges without recursion: pairs, then fours, then eights.

name: Natural merge sort
about: Merges the sorted runs already in the data instead of fixed-size blocks, so sorted input takes one pass.

name: In-place merge sort
about: Merges by rotating blocks instead of using a second array. It saves the memory and pays an extra log factor in moves.

name: Timsort
about: Tim Peters's 2002 sort for Python, later adopted by Java and Android for objects. Finds real runs and keeps merges balanced. This version leaves out galloping.

name: Powersort
about: Replaces Timsort's merge rules with a provably near-optimal order. CPython switched to it in version 3.11.

name: Strand sort
about: Pulls one increasing strand out of the data at a time and merges it into the result.

name: Patience sort
about: Deals items into piles by the rules of the card game patience, then merges the piles. The pile count equals the longest increasing subsequence.

name: Tournament sort
about: Runs a knockout bracket for the smallest item, then replays only the matches the winner was in.

name: Quicksort (Lomuto)
about: The textbook partition, with the last item as pivot. Hand it sorted data and it hits its worst case, which is worth watching.

name: Quicksort (Hoare)
about: Tony Hoare's original from 1959: two pointers walk inward and swap what's on the wrong side. Uses the middle item as pivot.

name: Quicksort (3-way)
about: Dijkstra's Dutch national flag partition: less than, equal to and greater than the pivot. Duplicates finish immediately.

name: Dual-pivot quicksort
about: Two pivots make three parts. Yaroslavskiy's 2009 idea became Java's built-in sort for primitive arrays.

name: Introsort
about: Quicksort that watches its own recursion depth and switches to heapsort if it goes too deep. The classic C++ std::sort.

name: Pattern-defeating quicksort
about: Orson Peters's quicksort, used in Go and for years in Rust. It spots sorted runs and bad pivots and adapts, without the faster block partition of the original.

name: Sample sort
about: Quicksort with 15 pivots at once, chosen from a sorted sample. The usual choice for sorting across many processors.

name: Heapsort
about: Builds a max-heap inside the array, then repeatedly moves the top to the end. Guaranteed n log n with no extra memory.

name: Ternary heapsort
about: Heapsort with three children per node: a shallower tree, but more comparisons at each level.

name: Bottom-up heapsort
about: Follows the larger child straight to a leaf, then climbs back to find the spot. Removed items nearly always belong near the bottom, so this saves comparisons.

name: Weak-heap sort
about: A loosened heap with one extra bit per node that makes comparisons close to the theoretical minimum.

name: Smoothsort
about: Dijkstra's 1981 heapsort over a forest of Leonardo trees. It approaches O(n) as the data gets closer to sorted.

name: Tree sort
about: Inserts everything into a plain binary search tree and reads it in order. Sorted input makes the tree a long chain.

name: AVL tree sort
about: Tree sort on the first self-balancing tree, from 1962. Rotations keep the tree shallow on any input.

name: Splay sort
about: Moves each new item to the root of the tree, so items near the last one inserted are cheap. Good on nearly sorted input.

name: Treap sort
about: A tree by key and a heap by random priority at once. Randomness alone keeps it balanced, whatever the input.

name: Cartesian tree sort
about: Builds a Cartesian tree in linear time, then uses a heap holding only the items that could come next. Fast when the data is nearly sorted.

name: Counting sort
about: Counts how many of each value there are, then writes them out in order. Never compares two items. k is the range of values.

name: Pigeonhole sort
about: Counting sort that keeps the items themselves in each hole, not just how many, so it can sort records.

name: Radix sort (LSD)
about: Stable-sorts by the last byte, then the next, up to the first. Punched-card machines sorted the same way. w is the number of bytes.

name: Radix sort (MSD)
about: Splits by the first byte, then sorts each group by the next. Small groups finish with insertion sort.

name: American flag sort
about: MSD radix sort done in place by following cycles of swaps, named for dividing an array into stripes.

name: Radix exchange sort
about: Quicksort where the pivot is a single bit: zeros go left, ones go right, then repeat on the next bit.

name: Bucket sort
about: Spreads items into n buckets by value and insertion-sorts each one. Linear when values are spread evenly.

name: Flashsort
about: Estimates each item's final position, moves it there in place by following cycles, then tidies up with insertion sort.

name: ProxmapSort
about: Maps each value to its likely neighbourhood in the output and insertion-sorts it into that small section as it arrives.

name: Interpolation sort
about: Bucket sort that recursively buckets each bucket, using the same idea as interpolation search.

name: Bead sort
about: Each number is a row of beads on an abacus, and gravity does the sorting. In hardware this could run in linear time. m is the largest value.

name: Batcher odd-even mergesort
about: A fixed wiring of comparisons from 1968. It does the same work on every input, so it can be built in hardware.

name: Bitonic sort
about: A sorting network built from up-then-down sequences, popular on GPUs.

name: Stooge sort
about: Sort the first two thirds, the last two thirds, then the first two thirds again. It works, and it's slower than bubble sort.

name: Slowsort
about: "Multiply and surrender", from a 1984 joke paper: the opposite of divide and conquer.

name: Bogosort
about: Shuffle. Is it sorted? No? Shuffle again.

name: Bozosort
about: Swap two random items. Is it sorted? No? Swap two more.
